claims.text: The Suez Canal lets ships travel between Europe and Asia without sailing around Africa.
The Panama Canal links the Atlantic and the Pacific, the Kiel Canal crosses northern Germany and the Corinth Canal crosses a Greek isthmus.

issues.note: Read literally, the Panama Canal also lets ships sail between Europe and Asia (East Asia and the Pacific) without going around Africa; it is a recognised if longer alternative for some voyages. The stem states an effect, not the link the canal makes, so a pedant can defend a second answer (card rule 2, guide 3.2). Reword to name the link, for example 'Which canal joins the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea?', or keep the shortcut idea with both seas named. The key claim changes, so it needs fresh checks.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: The search results agree that the Suez Canal is the shortest sea route between Europe and Asia, and they describe how it links the two seas. [...] The canal runs north to south across the Isthmus of Suez in Egypt, linking the Mediterranean and Red seas. [...] (It separates Africa from Asia, and it provides the shortest maritime route between Europe and the lands lying around the Indian and western Pacific oceans.) [...] Before the canal, ships bound for Asia had to sail around the southern tip of Africa, the Cape of Good Hope.

claimResults.note: Stated plainly. The summary names its sources only as a group (Britannica pages and the Suez Canal Authority's pages, Tier A and B), so the call counts at Tier B. It also fixes what 'without going around Africa' refers to: the Cape route that ships bound for Asia used before the canal.

claimResults.note: All three parts of c2 stated plainly; every result is Britannica (Tier B). The only differences the summary reports are Panama's length and transit time, which c2 does not state. This is the claim B's Panama reading disputes: see the second_answer issue.

issues.note: Ruling on B's second_answer (fix) about Panama: not a second answer. With external evidence now on both sides, the stem's 'without going around Africa' names the voyage the Suez Canal replaced (ships bound for Asia had to round the Cape of Good Hope before it opened, and it is the shortest sea route from Europe to the Indian and western Pacific oceans). The Panama Canal joins the Atlantic and the Pacific, so the voyage it spares is the one round South America; a ship heading west to East Asia through it was never going round Africa. I rate B's concern a note. If the editor wants no room at all for the literal reading, 'Which canal joins the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea?' closes it, but that changes the stem and needs fresh checks (§9.7).

Explanation, optional: 'Unlike the Panama Canal, it needs no locks, because the seas at its two ends lie at almost the same level' can be read as saying Panama has locks because its two oceans stand at different levels, whereas (my knowledge, not re-checked here) its locks lift ships over high ground between them. c3 and c4 were not in dispute and were not re-checked in this tiebreak.
